cards.title: Define the brand as a promise and expectation shortcut
cards.summary: Reframe branding from logos and mass advertising to a specific promise that shortcuts customer expectations.
cards.use_when: Deciding what your store's brand actually stands for before running awareness campaigns or redesigning assets.
steps: Write down the single promise your store makes to customers — what they can expect every time they buy from you (quality level, speed, vibe, values).
Audit whether every touchpoint (PDP copy, packaging, email tone, return policy) reinforces that promise or contradicts it.
Treat the logo and visual identity as downstream of the promise, not the starting point. Pixel-polishing a logo without a distinct promise is wasted effort.
Position the brand toward a specific tribe rather than a safe, average compromise for the mass market; a brand for everyone signals nothing to anyone.
Accept that brand marketing is largely unmeasurable cultural engagement, and keep it separate from your measurable funnel math.
caveats: Source treats brand awareness as culturally engaged but not directly measurable; do not expect clean ROI attribution from brand spend.
This card is about promise and positioning, not direct-response measurement.

cards.title: Map positioning on an extreme emotional XY grid
cards.summary: Use unconventional emotional axes (not price vs features) to find a defensible positioning space.
cards.use_when: Choosing how to differentiate your store or product line in a crowded category.
steps: Pick two extreme emotional attributes your category actually competes on — for example speed vs security, or status vs convenience.
Plot competitors on the two axes to see where the crowded middle sits; the middle is usually where undifferentiated brands die.
Choose a corner position that is extreme on at least one axis rather than a balanced compromise.
Define the brand promise so it clearly attracts the customers who want that extreme and repels the ones who don't.
Use the chosen position to guide merchandising, PDP messaging, and which product attributes you lead with — not just ads.
Revisit the grid when you add categories; an extreme position can carry across lines or may need its own grid.
caveats: Source uses these as strategic frames, not quantified scores; the axes are chosen judgment calls, not measured data.
An extreme position intentionally repels some buyers; that exclusion is the point, not a flaw.

cards.title: Use semiotics and vernacular to signal tribe belonging
cards.summary: Deliberate symbols, category vernacular, and visual cues attract the right tribe and filter out the wrong people.
cards.use_when: Designing PDP imagery, packaging, tone of voice, or ad creative that should signal who the product is for.
steps: Identify the trusted visual and verbal patterns your target tribe already recognizes in the category (source example draws on cues like driving gloves with holes or car wheel flares).
Embed those recognizable signifiers in your product photography, copy, and design rather than inventing unfamiliar signals.
Use intentional signals to attract insiders and repel outsiders — the source cites spam with deliberate bad grammar as a filter that selects only the gullible.
Match tone and vernacular to the tribe's own language so the store feels like 'people like us' rather than an outsider.
Audit existing assets for signals that attract the wrong audience or dilute the tribe signal.
Keep symbols coherent across PDP, email, packaging, and ads so the signal compounds.
caveats: Semiotic choices are interpretive and category-specific; what signals insider status in one tribe reads as noise or offense in another.
Over-filtering can shrink your addressable audience — the source treats this as a feature, but confirm demand exists.

cards.title: Price as a status and value story
cards.summary: Use price architecture to communicate status, protect margin, and avoid the race to the bottom.
cards.use_when: Setting or restructuring pricing and tier architecture for products or bundles.
steps: Decide what story the price tells: high price signals status and exclusivity; low price signals accessibility or convenience.
Build tiers (or a flagship plus entry product) so price itself communicates a ladder of status or value rather than a single commodity number.
Protect margin by positioning on the extreme axes (status, speed, identity) instead of competing purely on price.
Avoid discounting as a default lever; the source frames race-to-the-bottom pricing as a positioning failure, not a tactic.
Make the price story consistent with semiotic signals and the X Y position so price, symbols, and promise reinforce each other.
For bundles, use the price of components and the bundle together to signal relative value and status.
caveats: Status pricing only works when the rest of the brand supports the claim; a high price with weak signals reads as arbitrary.
The source treats price as narrative, not as a calculated willingness-to-pay study; validate demand before committing.

cards.title: Separate unmeasurable brand marketing from measurable direct marketing
cards.summary: Keep cultural brand engagement and ROI-tracked direct response in distinct buckets with distinct expectations.
cards.use_when: Allocating budget between brand-building campaigns and paid direct-response ads.
steps: Classify each campaign as brand (engages culture, largely unmeasurable) or direct (click tracking, funnel math, ROI).
For every direct-marketing action, require measurement of cost of attention against conversion yield through the funnel — if you cannot measure it, do not run the ad.
Do not justify unmeasured advertising by assuming awareness will pay for itself; treat that as an unsupported assumption.
Track bought attention strictly: cost per click versus yield of conversion across the funnel.
Compare lifetime value of the customers acquired against acquisition cost and scale ad spend only when LTV exceeds acquisition cost through the funnel.
Before buying more ads, fix a broken funnel by removing steps and supporting the customer's dreams and fears.
caveats: Source states the LTV-versus-acquisition-cost relationship as a rule but does not supply a numeric benchmark; compute your own LTV from repeat purchases, referrals, and network effects.
Source dismisses 'passive income' funnel myths that ignore the high cost of paid attention in a cluttered market.

cards.title: Treat your email list as an owned permission asset
cards.summary: Earn consensual, anticipated communication with a tribe rather than renting attention from platforms.
cards.use_when: Building or managing email/SMS lifecycle communication and deciding what to send.
steps: Earn permission by delivering on the exact promise made at enrollment — subscribers should get what they opted in for, not random blasts.
Apply the source's test for permission: communicate with people who would miss you if you didn't reach out.
Never spam, rent, or sell the list; treat it as a closely guarded owned asset.
Shift from being a 'sharecropper' on rented social media land to owning direct contact with your tribe.
Communicate drip by drip, keeping messages anticipated, personal, and relevant rather than interruptive.
Do not interrupt strangers without enrollment; interruptive cold direct marketing is a different activity with different rules.
caveats: The permission standard is a source opinion and stricter than legal compliance; it is a brand asset strategy, not a legal test.
Purchased lists, spam tactics, and interruption without enrollment defeat the permission model.

cards.title: Define the smallest viable market by worldview
cards.summary: Target a narrow psychographic cohort rather than a demographic mass market.
cards.use_when: Narrowing your target customer for product selection, messaging, and creative.
steps: Choose the smallest market that can sustain your business rather than trying to reach everyone.
Define 'people like us' by the stories they tell themselves, not by age, gender, or location.
Map the customer's worldview, internal narratives, and the specific fears or dreams that drive their behavior.
Separate early adopters (neophiliacs craving the new) from the mass market (adapters who want safety), and pick which you are serving.
Build avatar records that group people by their self-narrative and status driver, not by surface demographics.
Use the worldview to guide product selection, PDP framing, and ad hooks.
caveats: Source frames the mass market as the wrong target for early positioning; this is a strategic stance, not a universal rule.
Fictional personas without an underlying emotional job or status driver are explicitly called out as a failure mode.

cards.title: Write the three-sentence marketing promise
cards.summary: Use the source's template to state audience worldview, desired outcome, and the promise of your product.
cards.use_when: Drafting or tightening a positioning statement for a store, product line, or landing page.
steps: Fill the template: 'My product is for people who believe [X]. I will focus on people who want [Y]. I promise that engaging with what I make will help you get [Z].'
Fill X with the customer's worldview or belief, not a demographic.
Fill Y with the desired outcome or aspiration the customer is pursuing.
Fill Z with the concrete transformation your product enables.
Test the statement against your PDP headline, ad hooks, and email onboarding copy to check alignment.
Revise any touchpoint that lacks a clear X, Y, or Z connection.
caveats: The template is a source-provided heuristic, not a validated conversion device; test its effect on your own pages.
Belief and aspiration must be real for the target tribe; a fabricated worldview reads as generic marketing.

cards.title: Map status drivers: affiliation vs dominion
cards.summary: Identify whether your customers measure status by belonging (affiliation) or by winning and power (dominion).
cards.use_when: Choosing messaging, imagery, and bundle structure that appeals to your avatar's status motive.
steps: Determine for your target cohort whether status is measured through affiliation (connection and belonging) or dominion (power and winning).
Use the source's observation that status cues differ — for example who eats first versus who sits closest — to find your category's equivalent status signals.
Align product imagery, copy, and community features to the dominant status driver rather than mixing both.
Apply status logic to merchandising: exclusive tiers and leaderboards appeal to dominion; community, rituals, and shared identity appeal to affiliation.
Map decision trigger moments to the status role, since purchases often fire when status is at stake.
Recheck the driver when you enter a new segment; the same product can serve opposite status motives in different tribes.
caveats: Status orientation is a source framework, not a measured psychometric score; infer it from behavior and language.
Assuming a single driver for a broad audience risks misfiring; validate with customer research.

cards.title: Discover objections and the internal narrative that blocks purchase
cards.summary: Surface the cognitive dissonance and fear of change behind a prospect's 'no' before optimizing the offer.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing why qualified traffic fails to convert at cart or checkout.
steps: Identify the internal narrative the prospect tells themselves about the product and category.
List the specific fears of change and cognitive dissonance that cause prospects to say no.
Address those objections directly in PDP copy, FAQ, guarantees, and checkout reassurance.
Check whether your funnel steps themselves create friction or amplify fear; the source advises removing steps and supporting dreams and fears before buying more ads.
Do not treat objection handling as persuasion only — reduce perceived risk and effort where possible.
Re-test conversion after changes to see whether the narrative, not the traffic, was the constraint.
caveats: Objection discovery is qualitative; the source does not provide a quantitative threshold for how many objections to address.
Over-promising to dissolve fear can conflict with the brand promise and create returns or refund issues.

cards.title: Match message to market sophistication: early adopters vs mass
cards.summary: Decide whether you are selling to neophiliacs craving the new or adapters who want safety, and adjust the pitch.
cards.use_when: Choosing creative angle, feature emphasis, and guarantee strength for a launch or campaign.
steps: Classify your current audience as early adopters (neophiliacs who crave the new) or mass market (adapters who want safety).
For early adopters, lead with novelty, being first, and the edge of what's new.
For the mass market, lead with safety, reliability, proof, and reduction of risk.
Align channel and creative accordingly — a novelty hook that works on adopters may scare adapters and vice versa.
Sequence adoption: use early adopters to validate the product before repositioning toward the safety-seeking mass market.
Track which cohort converts so you do not mix the two messages in one campaign.
caveats: The distinction is a source framing of adoption stages, not a measured segmentation; validate with your own conversion data.
Moving from early adopters to mass market usually requires changing proof and risk-reduction, not just budget.

input.text:
04-BRD / brand Goes here. Brand as a shorthand for the customer's expectations and the promise you make. Positioning using an XY grid based on extreme emotional attributes. The use of semiotics, symbols, and vernacular to signal belonging to a specific tribe. The strategic use of pricing to tell a story about status and value. The distinction between unmeasurable brand marketing (which engages the culture) and measurable direct marketing. Not here. • Direct marketing measurement, click tracking, and funnel math -> 06-MEA • Individual customer psychographics and avatar creation -> 02-AVT

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Redefines branding from logos and mass advertising to extreme XY positioning, semiotic signaling, and pricing stories designed to unite a specific tribe.

modules: [BRD]

topics: [brand marketing vs direct marketing, semiotics, XY positioning, pricing strategy, symbols]

tier: 2

scope_hint: growth

Topics. brand book schema / defining the brand as a promise and expectation shortcut rather than just a logo; visual identity / semiotics, symbols, and category vernacular that remind the audience of trusted patterns (e.g., driving gloves with holes, car wheel flares); positioning / XY grid mapping using extreme emotional attributes (e.g., speed vs. security, status vs. convenience); pricing / price as a story, signaling status, creating margin, and avoiding the race to the bottom. Look for. XY positioning grids using unconventional axes rather than just price and features. Strategic semiotic choices that intentionally send signals to attract the right people and repel the wrong ones (e.g., Nigerian spam intentionally using bad grammar to filter for the gullible). Skip. Obsessing over logo design pixels at the expense of the brand promise. Attempts to position the brand as a safe, average compromise for the mass market. Scope mix. 20% baseline (having a distinct promise), 80% growth (XY positioning, pricing architecture, and semiotic signaling). Volume. 300 to 400.

02-AVT / avatars and jobs to be done Goes here. Moving beyond generic demographics to target the "smallest viable market" using psychographics. Understanding customer worldviews, internal narratives, and the specific fears or dreams that drive their behavior. Identifying how people measure their status through either affiliation (connection and belonging) or dominion (power and winning). Not here. • Plotting these emotional attributes on a competitive market matrix -> 04-BRD • Calculating the lifetime value of this specific avatar -> 06-MEA

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Shifts avatar creation from generic demographics to deep psychographics based on status, tension, and the specific worldview of the smallest viable market.

modules: [AVT]

topics: [smallest viable market, psychographics, worldviews, status roles, internal narratives]

tier: 1

scope_hint: baseline

Topics. research method / identifying the smallest viable market and defining "people like us"; market sophistication / early adopters (neophiliacs who crave the new) versus the mass market (adapters who want safety); objection discovery / understanding the internal narrative, cognitive dissonance, and fear of change that causes prospects to say no; jobs and trigger moments / mapping decisions to status roles (affiliation vs. dominion); avatar record structure / grouping people by the stories they tell themselves rather than what they look like. Look for. Specific definitions of a cohort's worldview and how they measure status (e.g., who eats first versus who sits closest). The explicit three-sentence marketing promise template: "My product is for people who believe [X]. I will focus on people who want [Y]. I promise that engaging with what I make will help you get [Z].". Skip. Broad demographic targets attempting to reach "everyone" or the "mass market". Fictional personas that lack an underlying emotional job or status driver. Scope mix. 100% baseline (defining the audience and their worldview is a universal prerequisite). Volume. 300 to 400.

06-MEA / measurement and economics Goes here. Funnel math, calculating the lifetime value (LTV) of a customer, and the strict economics of direct marketing. Tracking the cost of earning attention (clicks) versus the yield of a conversion. Not here. • Unmeasurable cultural brand advertising -> 04-BRD • The creative hooks and ads driving the initial clicks -> 10-MCR

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Clearly separates measurable direct-response funnel math from unmeasurable brand marketing, demanding strict ROI tracking for bought attention.

modules: [MEA]

topics: [funnel math, lifetime value (LTV), direct marketing measurement, cost of acquisition]

tier: 1

scope_hint: baseline

Topics. profit and contribution formulas / determining customer lifetime value (LTV), including network effects, repeat purchases, and referral value; incrementality / measuring the cost of a click versus the conversion yield through the funnel; tracking / the strict requirement to measure all direct marketing actions. Look for. The explicit mathematical relationship between LTV and ad spend: if LTV is higher than the cost to acquire a customer through the funnel, scale the ad spend. Rules for fixing a broken funnel (e.g., removing steps, supporting dreams/fears) before buying more ads. Skip. Brand marketing metrics or assumptions that unmeasured awareness ads will pay for themselves. "Passive income" funnel myths that ignore the high cost of paid attention in a cluttered market. Scope mix. 100% baseline (if you buy direct ads, you must measure everything; if you cannot measure it, do not run the ad). Volume. 200 to 300.

14-EML / email lifecycle Goes here. Permission marketing and earning the privilege to deliver anticipated, personal, and relevant messages. Building an owned asset to communicate directly with your tribe rather than renting attention from social media platforms. Not here. • Interruptive direct marketing ads to cold audiences -> 11-ADC • Brand awareness publicity and PR -> 04-BRD

Header.

url:

rights: public_reference

why: Defines email marketing not as blasting spam, but as managing a closely guarded permission asset built on anticipated, consensual, and relevant communication.

modules: [EML]

topics: [permission marketing, owned assets, anticipated messaging, enrollment]

tier: 2

scope_hint: baseline

Topics. permission acquisition / earning the right to contact people without a middleman; list management / treating the list as a valuable asset and never spamming, renting, or selling it; engagement / delivering on the exact promise made during enrollment and communicating drip by drip. Look for. The strict definition of permission: communicating only with "people who would miss you if you didn't reach out". The strategic transition from acting as a "sharecropper" on rented social media land to owning a direct-contact permission asset. Skip. Spam tactics, purchasing email lists, or strategies relying on interrupting strangers without enrollment. Scope mix. 100% baseline (permission is a mandatory requirement for lifecycle marketing). Volume. 200 to 300.
